source: Mohanani, Salman, Turhan, Rodriguez, Ralph (2020) Cognitive Biases in Software Engineering: A Systematic Mapping Study
finding: Systematic mapping of the SE bias literature up to 2016. Search found 826 articles, 308 duplicates removed, 40 primary studies, 16 from snowballing, 9 from author lists, 1 from bias-name search: 66 found, 65 analysed.
numbers: 65 articles (1990-2016), 37 biases. Most studied: anchoring 26, confirmation 23, overconfidence 16. 72% (47) empirical, 28% (18) non-empirical. Most empirical work is lab experiments.
quote: Cognitive biases are systematic deviations from optimal reasoning.
limits: Mapping, not meta-analysis: no pooled effect sizes. Inter-rater agreement was mediocre (55% on one step). Search ended 2016.
agent_relevance: Baseline for G3: SE bias research is mostly about people, so the agent analogue must be tested on the agent itself.

source: Mohanani, Salman, Turhan, Rodriguez, Ralph (2020) Cognitive Biases in Software Engineering: A Systematic Mapping Study
finding: Debiasing evidence is almost absent. Techniques cover only 6 of 37 biases and none of the primary studies gives strong empirical evidence that any technique works. All are untested suggestions.
numbers: 6 of 37 biases have any debiasing proposal. 0 studies with strong effectiveness evidence.
quote: None of the research reviewed here provides compelling empirical evidence that any specific debiasing approach will be effective
limits: Authors also warn debiasing can have unintended consequences. Written pre-2017.
agent_relevance: Do not borrow a human debiasing trick (warnings, awareness) as if proven; prefer task redesign enforced by code (Fischhoff: debias the task, not the person).

source: Mohanani, Salman, Turhan, Rodriguez, Ralph (2020) Cognitive Biases in Software Engineering: A Systematic Mapping Study
finding: Confirmation bias in testing: testers and developers pick tests that show the program works rather than tests that could show failure ('positive test bias'). Specification completeness, domain knowledge and presence of errors moderate it. Programming expertise seemed to have no effect (P31). Confirmation bias in testing was linked to more production defects (P4, P6).
numbers: Based on primary studies P4, P6, P31, P32 as summarised; no numbers given in the review itself.
quote: developers tend to test their programs with data that is consistent with 'the way that the program is supposed to work'
limits: Review-level summary of other authors' studies; direction of causation to defects not established.
agent_relevance: Direct basis for G3: a pass must come from a test aimed to fail the answer, not from tests that fit it.

source: Mohanani, Salman, Turhan, Rodriguez, Ralph (2020) Cognitive Biases in Software Engineering: A Systematic Mapping Study
finding: The only logic-training result in the review: participants trained in logical reasoning and hypothesis testing showed less confirmation bias in software testing (P4 = Calikli and Bener). Professionals experienced but inactive as developer/testers showed less bias than those experienced and active.
numbers: No numbers in the review. Source study detail in lines a05 to a10.
quote: Participants who have been trained in logical reasoning and hypothesis testing skills manifested less confirmation bias in software testing
limits: Correlational and quasi-experimental (groups differ in many ways); no randomised training trial. Summaries often overstate this as 'logic training reduced bias'.
agent_relevance: Training effect is not shown causally. For an agent, build the falsification step into the scaffold rather than rely on a skill.

source: Calikli and Bener (2010) Empirical analysis of factors affecting confirmation bias levels of software engineers (PPIG 22)
finding: Participants did two tests based on Wason tasks: a pen-and-paper test (selection-task style, abstract, thematic and software-domain questions) and an interactive replication of Wason's rule discovery task. Scored with the Reich and Ruth falsifier/verifier/matcher method plus Wason's eliminative/enumerative index and test severity.
numbers: N=88: telecom company C1 n=34 (11 F, 23 M, mean age 29.06); small firms C2 n=6, C3 n=8, C4 n=12; graduate computer engineering students n=28 (mean age 27.96).
limits: Convenience samples, tests in work settings for firms and at university for students. Different conditions across groups (rush stress is acknowledged).
agent_relevance: Shows how to measure falsification tendency with a Wason-style probe; a similar probe could audit the agent's own test choices.

source: Calikli and Bener (2010) Empirical analysis of factors affecting confirmation bias levels of software engineers (PPIG 22)
finding: Experience did not predict hypothesis-testing skill. No significant correlation between years of testing experience (n=27) or development experience (n=50) and test severity or the eliminative/enumerative index.
numbers: testing experience n=27 and development experience n=50: no significant correlations with test severity or elimination index.
limits: Years of experience is a crude proxy. Matches the review's note that programming expertise had no effect on confirmation bias (P31).
agent_relevance: Fluency or seniority does not remove positive-test bias; a strong model is not exempt by capability alone.

source: Calikli and Bener (2010) Empirical analysis of factors affecting confirmation bias levels of software engineers (PPIG 22)
finding: Company size effect on the interactive test: the large telecom company did better at elimination than the small and medium firms. No difference on abstract logic questions, and no significant difference in insight categories.
numbers: Eliminative/enumerative index Mann-Whitney z=-2.76, p<.01 (C1 n=34 mean rank 35.47 vs small firms n=26 mean rank 23.06). Test severity z=-2.26, p<.05 (ranks 34.96 vs 24.67). C1 vs C2 alone: severity z=-2.48 p<.05, elimination z=-3.82 p<.001.
limits: Group differences could reflect selection or job type, not training. Non-parametric tests on small groups.
agent_relevance: Hypothesis-testing behaviour varies with setting; it is not a fixed trait.

source: Calikli and Bener (2010) Empirical analysis of factors affecting confirmation bias levels of software engineers (PPIG 22)
finding: Students (more abstract training, less work experience) did better than company employees on hypothesis testing overall, per the authors. They infer that continuous use of abstract reasoning and logic training lowers confirmation bias. This is the source of the 'logic training reduced confirmation bias' claim.
numbers: Employees (n=43, above-student experience) vs students (n=13): the only reported significant difference was interactive test duration, z=-1.39, p<.05 (student rank 23.04 vs 30.15; students finished faster).
quote: Hence, we conclude that there is a relationship between confirmation bias and continuous usage of and training in logical reasoning and critical thinking.
limits: Inference to training is an interpretation of group differences, not a trained-vs-control experiment. The one stated significant employee/student difference is test duration.
agent_relevance: Weak support for 'logic training'. Treat the claim as single-source [S].

source: Calikli and Bener (2010) Empirical analysis of factors affecting confirmation bias levels of software engineers (PPIG 22)
finding: Developer defect link, tiny sample. Of 12 developers and 16 testers on a telecom project, only 5 developers had churn data. The developer who gave up the interactive test had the highest defect ratio.
numbers: Defect ratio (defective files / files written): Developer1 0.86 (aborted interactive test), D2 0.38, D3 0.20, D4 0.00, D5 0.11. Authors say more data are needed for statistical significance.
quote: there is a direct correlation between confirmation bias and defect proneness of the code
limits: n=5, no significance test, and the elimination index of D1 (0.83) did not clearly differ from others. The 'direct correlation' claim is not statistically supported in this paper.
agent_relevance: Do not cite as proof that biased testing causes defects; it is a case sketch.

source: Calikli and Bener (2010) Empirical analysis of factors affecting confirmation bias levels of software engineers (PPIG 22)
finding: Tester link, also small. Of 16 testers only 12 had performance data. Among testers who reported more bugs than average there were no falsifiers and more verifiers; among testers who caused above-average production defects there were also no falsifiers. Reported bugs and production defects correlated at Spearman 0.8234.
numbers: 12 testers; Spearman rho 0.8234 between bugs reported and production defects.
limits: Number of bugs found is also a function of how many bugs exist. Data from one project at one firm.
agent_relevance: Bias metrics may hide trade-offs: high bug counts can come with missed severe defects.

source: Sovrano, Dominici, Sevastjanova, Stramiglio, Bacchelli (2025) Is General-Purpose AI Reasoning Sensitive to Data-Induced Cognitive Biases? PROBE-SWE
finding: First dynamic benchmark of human-style SE biases in LLMs. 16 hand-written seed tasks, 8 biases (including anchoring and confirmation), each with a biased and unbiased twin that share the same logic (checked with Prolog). Measure: how often the model flips its decision when the bias cue is added.
numbers: Models: GPT, LLaMA, DeepSeek families. All showed sensitivity. Average sensitivity from 5.9% (anchoring) to 35.3% (hindsight). 300 dilemmas per bias. Human check: 98.5% of sampled dilemmas valid; mean raw agreement 0.887 but Fleiss kappa only 0.194.
limits: Synthetic dilemmas made by LLMs. Sensitivity depends on which model generated the data (anchoring above 11% on DeepSeek-made data, near 0% on others). Prolog covers only rule-like reasoning.
agent_relevance: Anchoring is the weakest effect in models; hindsight and hyperbolic discounting are strong. Paired biased/unbiased probes can audit our agent.

source: Sovrano, Dominici, Sevastjanova, Stramiglio, Bacchelli (2025) Is General-Purpose AI Reasoning Sensitive to Data-Induced Cognitive Biases? PROBE-SWE
finding: Bias sensitivity grows with reasoning complexity for most biases, so harder SE problems make the model more prone to shortcut cues. Awareness of bias does not mean resistance to it.
numbers: Change per higher complexity tier: confirmation +33.66 pp (CI 25.5-41.8, p<.001), framing +23.10, availability +9.81, bandwagon +8.84, anchoring +3.77 pp (CI 2.2-5.3). Decreases: hindsight -17.25, hyperbolic discounting -17.70. Overconfidence no effect (p=0.76). Bias awareness 52% (GPT-4.1-mini) to 80% (GPT-4o-mini).
limits: Complexity measured as Prolog inference steps. Tiers unbalanced per bias. Awareness measured by a judge.
agent_relevance: Confirmation effect rises sharply with task difficulty, exactly when G3 matters most. Recognising a bias is not the same as controlling it.

source: Sovrano, Dominici, Sevastjanova, Stramiglio, Bacchelli (2025) Is General-Purpose AI Reasoning Sensitive to Data-Induced Cognitive Biases? PROBE-SWE
finding: Authors' own mitigation advice: bias-aware instructions, cross-check against a symbolic oracle before the final choice, self-consistency penalising bias-conditioned flips, and training-time regularisation. Not tested in this paper.
numbers: No mitigation experiment run; only suggestions.
limits: Suggestions, not results. Larger or longer-reasoning models did not uniformly reduce sensitivity.
agent_relevance: Supports our design choice: code-side checks, not model self-warnings.

source: Zhou, Saghi, Sabouri, Pandita, McGuire, Chattopadhyay (2026) Cognitive Biases in LLM-Assisted Software Development (ICSE 2026)
finding: Observation of 14 developers (student and professional) coding with an LLM, 2,013 actions, plus survey of 22 developers. Coded against a taxonomy of 90 biases in 15 categories (from 239 candidate biases, reviewed by psychologists). Extends Chattopadhyay et al. 2020.
numbers: 2,013 actions; 808 (40.2%) involved the LLM. 983 (48.8%) linked to a bias. Of LLM actions, 456 of 808 (56.4%) had at least one bias. 393 of 983 biased actions had multiple biases.
limits: Small sample (14), qualitative coding, mixed students and professionals. Human developers, not agents.
agent_relevance: Human-AI code review is bias-prone; the evaluator role is where confirmation and anchoring appear.

source: Zhou, Saghi, Sabouri, Pandita, McGuire, Chattopadhyay (2026) Cognitive Biases in LLM-Assisted Software Development (ICSE 2026)
finding: LLM-related actions were more often biased and more often reversed than non-LLM actions. Fixation (anchoring-type) biases led to the most reversals.
numbers: LLM actions biased 53.71% (434/808); reversed 29.46% (238/808); overall reversal 25% (505/2013). Fixation reversal 43.4%. Belief confirmation: 77 LLM actions, 26 reversed (33.8%).
limits: Chi-square tests with Bonferroni correction. Reversal defined by authors' coding.
agent_relevance: Anchoring on an LLM's first answer is a human-side failure; our agent should show alternatives, not one answer.

source: Zhou, Saghi, Sabouri, Pandita, McGuire, Chattopadhyay (2026) Cognitive Biases in LLM-Assisted Software Development (ICSE 2026)
finding: Partial replication of Chattopadhyay et al. (ICSE 2020): the bias rate is similar but the bias-reversal link did not replicate. Prior study: 45.72% of 2,084 actions biased; reversal 52.9% (1,104/2,084); 79.64% (759/953) of biased actions reversed.
numbers: This study: 47.14% (949/2,013) of actions associated with a bias, close to 45.72%. Reversal only 25%. Biased actions reversed 27.08% (257/949). Chi-square: no significant bias-reversal association (p=0.058, Bonferroni threshold 0.016).
limits: Different setting (LLM-assisted vs classic IDE) and coding schemes, so a boundary condition rather than a clean failure to replicate. Original paper not opened here.
agent_relevance: Frequency of biased actions is robust; their cost (reversal) is not.

source: Jones and Steinhardt (2022) Capturing Failures of Large Language Models via Human Cognitive Biases
finding: Anchoring test on Codex and CodeGen: prepend a similar but wrong 'anchor function' (print-var or add-var lines) to HumanEval prompts. Accuracy drops and anchor lines leak into answers, even into correct solutions.
numbers: Codex generated 'for var in' in 32%-61% of solutions and print(var) in 26%-44% when at least one canonical line was included. Anchor lines appeared in correct solutions: 3%-11% for the loop. Verbatim copy of the anchor function only 7%-12% (Codex) and 4%-12% (CodeGen) for add-var.
limits: Codex and CodeGen (older models). Effect shown across several numbers of canonical lines; no human baseline.
agent_relevance: Code models anchor on earlier in-context code: do not leave a failed attempt in the prompt when sampling a new one.

source: Jones and Steinhardt (2022) Capturing Failures of Large Language Models via Human Cognitive Biases
finding: Framing test: adding an irrelevant preceding function with a bad return line lowers accuracy, and the model copies the line.
numbers: Accuracy lost 22.3 to 30.5 points (Codex). Framing line reproduced in 81% of Codex outputs and 70.7% of CodeGen outputs, versus 4.5% and 0.0% on unmodified prompts.
limits: Five hand-chosen framing lines; synthetic prompts.
agent_relevance: Irrelevant context acts as an anchor even when it contradicts the type signature.

source: Jones and Steinhardt (2022) Capturing Failures of Large Language Models via Human Cognitive Biases
finding: Availability-heuristic test and attribute substitution: models favour frequent training patterns and follow function names over specs.
numbers: Unary-first vs binary-first operations: Codex accuracy 50% -> 17% when order flipped; 75% of the wrong binary-first outputs were the unary-first solution. Conflicting function name: accuracy 100% -> 4.4-4.6%; Codex followed the name in 52%-80% of prompts.
limits: 12 operation combinations; small controlled set; Codex only.
agent_relevance: Surface cues beat the stated requirement; tests should vary names and orders (mutations) to catch this.

source: Jones and Steinhardt (2022) Capturing Failures of Large Language Models via Human Cognitive Biases
finding: Replication of Jacowitz and Kahneman (1995) anchoring on GPT-3 davinci-001: 14 of 15 original questions, anchors set at 20% or 50% above and below the true answer.
numbers: Anchor +/-20%: no change 10.7%, toward anchor 28.6%, away 10.7%, gibberish 50.0%. Anchor +/-50%: no change 14.3%, toward 42.9%, away 10.7%, gibberish 32.1%. Estimate equalled the anchor 67% of the time.
quote: Our replication has a few limitations. Like the original study our sample size is small
limits: Small sample, templated prompts, mean 41% gibberish. Old model. Human anchor values not re-run.
agent_relevance: Numeric anchoring appears in LMs and grows with anchor size; ask for estimates before showing any prior number.

source: Echterhoff, Liu, Alessa, McAuley, He (2024) Cognitive Bias in Decision-Making with LLMs (BiasBuster)
finding: Dataset of 13,465 prompts testing prompt-induced, sequential and inherent biases (anchoring, status quo, framing, group attribution, primacy) in student admission decisions. Proposes 'selfhelp': the model rewrites its own prompt to remove bias cues.
numbers: Selfhelp left 0% (Llama 2 13B) and 1.4% (Llama 2 7B) of framing-biased prompts; GPT-4 group-attribution elements to 0% and framing to 2.7%. For anchoring, when allowed to revise, Llama models changed 40-52% of their decisions.
limits: Admissions decisions, not code. Anchoring selfhelp worked only for high-capacity models.
agent_relevance: Self-debiasing works by editing the input, but only for strong models; weaker models flip answers too often.

source: Lampinen, Dasgupta, Chan, Sheahan, Creswell, Kumaran, McClelland, Hill (2024) Language models show human-like content effects on reasoning tasks
finding: Tested LMs and humans on natural language inference, syllogisms and the Wason selection task (the confirmation-bias paradigm). Both do better when content matches belief, and both are poor at abstract Wason rules.
numbers: Humans did not beat chance on the Wason task overall. Realistic-rule advantage significant in humans, Chinchilla, PaLM 2-L and GPT-3.5 (all z>2.2, p<0.03); only marginal in PaLM 2-M and Flan-PaLM 2 (z<=1.78, p>=0.08). Human accuracy rose with response time (z=4.44, p<0.001).
limits: Prompting details affect results. Models differ from humans in the pattern of card choices.
agent_relevance: Confirmation-style errors in LMs depend on content: abstract or neutral probes expose them best.

source: Liu, Xia, Wang, Zhang (2023) Is Your Code Generated by ChatGPT Really Correct? (EvalPlus)
finding: Weak tests confirm wrong code. Adding 80x more tests to HumanEval (HumanEval+) uncovers wrong LLM code across 26 models and changes model rankings.
numbers: pass@k drops up to 19.3% (pass@1), 24.9% (pass@10), 28.9% (pass@100). CodeGen-16B -18.5%, CodeLlama-34B -17.6%, StarCoder -14.1%, ChatGPT -12.6%, GPT-4 -13.1%. Tests grown 80x; distilled mini set 47x smaller.
quote: HumanEval+ is able to catch significant amounts of previously undetected wrong code
limits: Reference solutions in HumanEval were also found wrong in some cases. Python function-level tasks only.
agent_relevance: Quantifies G3: a few given examples let wrong code pass; mutated or extra inputs catch it.

source: Itzhak, Stanovsky, Rosenfeld, Belinkov (2024) Instructed to Bias
finding: Studied decoy effect, certainty effect and belief bias in GPT-3, Mistral and T5 families. Found stronger bias in instruction-tuned models (Flan-T5, Mistral-Instruct, GPT-3.5, GPT-4).
numbers: Direction only from abstract and setup; no per-model numbers read here.
quote: we find a stronger presence of biases in models that have undergone instruction tuning
limits: Only the abstract and setup were read closely; belief bias is the logic-reasoning analogue of confirmation bias.
agent_relevance: Instruction tuning may increase bias; do not assume a chat-tuned judge is neutral.

source: Huang, Chen, Mishra, Zheng, Yu, Song, Zhou (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: Without outside feedback, asking an LLM to review its own answer does not help and can hurt. Evidence for G2.
numbers: GPT-3.5 on GSM8K: 75.9 standard and 75.9 after self-correction round 2 in the table read; the model kept its first answer 74.7% of the time and was more likely to flip correct to incorrect than the reverse.
quote: The fundamental issue is that LLMs cannot properly judge the correctness of their reasoning
limits: Intrinsic self-correction only; with oracle or external feedback it can help.
agent_relevance: Self-review is itself a confirmation-prone step; require code-side failing output (G2) before revision.

source: Mohanani, Salman, Turhan, Rodriguez, Ralph (2020) Cognitive Biases in Software Engineering: A Systematic Mapping Study
finding: Anchoring in SE: antecedents and effects. Experts less prone than novices (P16). Anchoring on a low initial completion estimate makes managers overrate productivity, leading to pressure and later extra resources. Developers anchor on the first understanding of requirements or design and adjust insufficiently.
numbers: 26 primary studies on anchoring. Debiasing suggestions: planning poker (P38), generating multiple designs (P33), directed questions (P3). All unevaluated.
quote: Developers then tend to adjust these anchors insufficiently to accommodate new or conflicting desiderata
limits: The term has widened beyond numeric estimates to any first piece of information, which weakens its precision.
agent_relevance: A first hypothesis is an anchor: keep the first candidate unseen when generating alternatives.

source: Mohanani, Salman, Turhan, Rodriguez, Ralph (2020) Cognitive Biases in Software Engineering: A Systematic Mapping Study
finding: Optimism bias studies: developers more optimistic than managers on web tasks (P50); students' confidence intervals too narrow (P52); asking 'how much effort for X' gave less optimistic estimates than 'how much can be done in Y hours' (P47). Reference class forecasting proposed (P45).
numbers: No pooled numbers in the review; study IDs only.
limits: Mostly estimation studies with students. Planning Poker targets anchoring but not optimism.
agent_relevance: Ask the agent for a base rate (reference class) before a self-estimate of success.

source: Mohanani, Salman, Turhan, Rodriguez, Ralph (2020) Cognitive Biases in Software Engineering: A Systematic Mapping Study
finding: Theory limits: cognitive biases are labels, not a theory. The review cites a critique that one-word labels such as availability, anchoring and representativeness say nothing about underlying processes.
numbers: Authors list confusions: biases vs heuristics, no compelling evidence for any debiasing method.
quote: the explanations of phenomena via one-word labels such as availability, anchoring, and representativeness are vague, insufficient
limits: Also: 200+ biases exist; terminology inconsistent across studies.
agent_relevance: Prefer concrete failure-mode checks (does the test try to fail?) over bias vocabulary in the schema.

source: Fischhoff (1982) Debiasing, as cited in Mohanani et al. 2020
finding: Fischhoff's escalation: warn, describe direction, give feedback, extended training, or debias the task instead of the person. Taken from Mohanani's quoted passage; Fischhoff's chapter itself was not opened.
numbers: Warnings and description are called 'rarely effective' in the cited text.
limits: Secondary citation only.
agent_relevance: Task redesign beats telling the model to be careful.

source: Chattopadhyay, Nelson, Au, Morales, Sanchez, Pandita, Sarma (2020) A tale from the trenches: cognitive biases and software development (ICSE)
finding: Observed developers at work and coded bias types. As reported by Zhou et al. 2026 (original not opened; ACM blocked): 45.72% of 2,084 actions were bias-associated, and biased actions were strongly tied to reversals.
numbers: 45.72% of 2,084 actions; reversal 52.9% (1,104/2,084); biased-and-reversed 79.64% (759/953). Figures taken from Zhou et al. 2026.
limits: Second-hand numbers.
agent_relevance: Original human baseline for the 2026 replication.
